title: BEKOS ET KOUTROPOULOS c. GRECE
summary:
In the case of Bekos and Koutropoulos v. Greece, the applicants, Mr. Lazaros Bekos and Mr. Eleftherios Koutropoulos, are Greek nationals of Roma origin residing in Missolonghi, western Greece. Their case highlights the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police violence and discrimination, particularly in situations of arrest and detention. On the night of 8 May 1998, following an attempted break-in at a kiosk, the two young Roma men were apprehended by police. They alleged that, after being handcuffed, they were subjected to repeated beatings, threats, and degrading treatment by several police officers both at the scene and later at the police station. The applicants also reported being insulted about their Roma origin and suffering physical injuries, which were documented by a forensic doctor the following day. Despite their complaints, the investigation into the police conduct was, according to the applicants, ineffective and insufficient, and they claimed to have been intimidated into withdrawing their complaints.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court declared the application admissible, finding that the allegations raised serious questions of fact and law requiring a full examination. This case is significant as it underscores the persistent challenges Roma and Travellers face in Europe regarding police abuse and the lack of effective remedies, reflecting a broader historical pattern of discrimination and marginalisation.
